00002| title: Proxy
00003| nav_title: Proxy
00004| description: Use Next.js Proxy to rewrite, redirect, modify headers, or respond directly before a request completes.
00005| related:
00006|   title: API Reference
00007|   description: Learn more about Proxy
00008|   links:
00009|     - app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy
00010|     - app/guides/backend-for-frontend
00011| ---
00012| 
00013| ## Proxy
00014| 
00015| > **Good to know**: Starting with Next.js 16, Middleware is now called Proxy to better reflect its purpose. The functionality remains the same.
00016| 
00017| Proxy allows you to run code before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
00018| 
00019| ### Use cases
00020| 
00021| Some common scenarios where Proxy is effective include:
00022| 
00023| - Modifying headers for all pages or a subset of pages
00024| - Rewriting to different pages based on A/B tests or experiments
00025| - Programmatic redirects based on incoming request properties
00026| 
00027| For simple redirects, consider using the [`redirects`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/redirects) configuration in `next.config.ts` first. Proxy should be used when you need access to request data or more complex logic.
00028| 
00029| Proxy is _not_ intended for slow data fetching. While Proxy can be helpful for [optimistic checks](/docs/app/guides/authentication#optimistic-checks-with-proxy-optional) such as permission-based redirects, it should not be used as a full session management or authorization solution.
00030| 
00031| Using fetch with `options.cache`, `options.next.revalidate`, or `options.next.tags`, has no effect in Proxy.
00032| 
00033| ### Convention
00034| 
00035| Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
00036| 
00037| > **Note**: While only one `proxy.ts` file is supported per project, you can still organize your proxy logic into modules. Break out proxy functionalities into separate `.ts` or `.js` files and import them into your main `proxy.ts` file. This allows for cleaner management of route-specific proxy, aggregated in the `proxy.ts` for centralized control. By enforcing a single proxy file, it simplifies configuration, prevents potential conflicts, and optimizes performance by avoiding multiple proxy layers.
00038| 
00039| ### Example
00040| 
00041| You can export your proxy function as either a default export or a named `proxy` export:
00042| 
00043| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00044| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00045| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00046| 
00047| // This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
00048| export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
00049|   return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
00050| }
00051| 
00052| // Alternatively, you can use a default export:
00053| // export default function proxy(request: NextRequest) { ... }
00054| 
00055| export const config = {
00056|   matcher: '/about/:path*',
00057| }
00058| ```
00059| 
00060| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00061| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00062| 
00063| // This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
00064| export function proxy(request) {
00065|   return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
00066| }
00067| 
00068| // Alternatively, you can use a default export:
00069| // export default function proxy(request) { ... }
00070| 
00071| export const config = {
00072|   matcher: '/about/:path*',
00073| }
00074| ```
00075| 
00076| The `matcher` config allows you to filter Proxy to run on specific paths. See the [Matcher](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#matcher) documentation for more details on path matching.
00077| 
00078| Read more about [using `proxy`](/docs/app/guides/backend-for-frontend#proxy), or refer to the `proxy` [API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy).
00079| 

(End of file - total 79 lines)

00073| The `matcher` option allows you to target specific paths for the Proxy to run on.
00074| 
00075| Without a `matcher`, Proxy runs on **every request**, including static files (`_next/static`), image optimizations (`_next/image`), and assets in the `public/` folder. Consider using a [negative match pattern](#negative-matching) to exclude these paths, otherwise auth logic or redirects can unintentionally block CSS, JS, or images from loading.
00076| 
00077| You can specify paths in several ways:
00078| 
00079| - For a single path: Directly use a string to define the path, like `'/about'`.
00080| - For multiple paths: Use an array to list multiple paths, such as `matcher: ['/about', '/contact']`, which applies the Proxy to both `/about` and `/contact`.
00081| 
00082| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00083| export const config = {
00084|   matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*'],
00085| }
00086| ```
00087| 
00088| Additionally, the `matcher` option supports complex path specifications using regular expressions. For example, you can exclude certain paths with a regular expression matcher:
00089| 
00090| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00091| export const config = {
00092|   matcher: [
00093|     // Exclude API routes, static files, image optimizations, and .png files
00094|     '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\\.png$).*)',
00095|   ],
00096| }
00097| ```
00098| 
00099| This enables precise control over which paths to include or exclude.
00100| 
00101| The `matcher` option accepts an array of objects with the following keys:
00102| 
00103| - `source`: The path or pattern used to match the request paths. It can be a string for direct path matching or a pattern for more complex matching.
00104| - `locale` (optional): A boolean that, when set to `false`, ignores locale-based routing in path matching.
00105| - `has` (optional): Specifies conditions based on the presence of specific request elements such as headers, query parameters, or cookies.
00106| - `missing` (optional): Focuses on conditions where certain request elements are absent, like missing headers or cookies.
00107| 
00108| ```js filename="proxy.js"
00109| export const config = {
00110|   matcher: [
00111|     {
00112|       source: '/api/:path*',
00113|       locale: false,
00114|       has: [
00115|         { type: 'header', key: 'Authorization', value: 'Bearer Token' },
00116|         { type: 'query', key: 'userId', value: '123' },
00117|       ],
00118|       missing: [{ type: 'cookie', key: 'session', value: 'active' }],
00119|     },
00120|   ],
00121| }
00122| ```
00123| 
00124| The `source` path patterns:
00125| 
00126| 1. MUST start with `/`
00127| 2. Can include named parameters: `/about/:path` matches `/about/a` and `/about/b` but not `/about/a/c`
00128| 3. Can have modifiers on named parameters (starting with `:`): `/about/:path*` matches `/about/a/b/c` because `*` is _zero or more_. `?` is _zero or one_ and `+` _one or more_
00129| 4. Can use regular expression enclosed in parenthesis: `/about/(.*)` is the same as `/about/:path*`
00130| 5. Are anchored to the start of the path: `/about` matches `/about` and `/about/team` but not `/blog/about`
00131| 
00132| Read more details on [path-to-regexp](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#path-to-regexp-1) documentation.
00133| 
00134| > **Good to know**:
00135| >
00136| > - The `matcher` values need to be constants so they can be statically analyzed at build-time. Dynamic values such as variables will be ignored.
00137| > - For backward compatibility, Next.js always considers `/public` as `/public/index`. Therefore, a matcher of `/public/:path` will match.
00138| 
00139| ## Params
00140| 
00141| Next.js calls the Proxy function with two arguments, [`request`](#request) and [`event`](#event), in that order. Declare only the ones you use.
00142| 
00143| ### `request`
00144| 
00145| The first parameter is an instance of `NextRequest`, which represents the incoming HTTP request.
00146| 
00147| ```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00148| import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00149| 
00150| export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
00151|   // Proxy logic goes here
00152| }
00153| ```
00154| 
00155| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00156| export function proxy(request) {
00157|   // Proxy logic goes here
00158| }
00159| ```
00160| 
00161| ### `event`
00162| 
00163| The second parameter is an instance of `NextFetchEvent`. It exposes a single method, `waitUntil(promise)`, which keeps the Proxy invocation alive until the promise settles, so background work like logging or analytics can finish after the response is sent. See [`waitUntil` and `NextFetchEvent`](#waituntil-and-nextfetchevent) for a full example.
00164| 
00165| ```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00166| import type { NextFetchEvent, NextRequest } from 'next/server'
00167| 
00168| export function proxy(request: NextRequest, event: NextFetchEvent) {
00169|   event.waitUntil(
00170|     fetch('https://example.com/log', {
00171|       method: 'POST',
00172|       body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname }),
00173|     })
00174|   )
00175| }
00176| ```
00177| 
00178| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00179| export function proxy(request, event) {
00180|   event.waitUntil(
00181|     fetch('https://example.com/log', {
00182|       method: 'POST',
00183|       body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname }),
00184|     })
00185|   )
00186| }
00187| ```
00188| 
00189| ### `NextProxy` type
00190| 
00191| If you prefer a shorthand, you can use the `NextProxy` type. It infers the parameter types for both `request` (`NextRequest`) and `event` (`NextFetchEvent`) automatically:
00192| 
00193| ```tsx filename="proxy.ts"
00194| import type { NextProxy } from 'next/server'
00195| 
00196| export const proxy: NextProxy = (request, event) => {
00197|   event.waitUntil(Promise.resolve())
00198|   return Response.json({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname })
00199| }
00200| ```

> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.

The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.

Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.

> **Good to know**:
>
> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
>
